items.stem: All of the following threatened Harry Truman’s chances for re-election in 1948 EXCEPT
options: Truman’s positions on civil rights
rampant inflation
the Dixiecrat candidacy of Strom Thurmond
public dissatisfaction with the Korean War
items.explanation: The Korean War didn’t begin until 1950.

option_explanations.A: Truman's civil-rights stands — including desegregating the armed forces in 1948 — genuinely alienated Southern Democrats and helped spark the Dixiecrat revolt, so this was a real threat, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Rampant postwar inflation genuinely hurt Truman's standing in 1948, so this was a real threat, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Strom Thurmond's Dixiecrat candidacy genuinely split the Democratic vote in 1948, so this was a real threat, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The Korean War did not begin until 1950, two years after the 1948 election. Public dissatisfaction with it could not have threatened Truman's 1948 re-election — this is the exception.

items.stem: Loyalty oaths, blacklists, and Alger Hiss are all associated with the
options: civil rights movement
New Deal
Red Scare
Great Society
items.explanation: Fear of communist infiltration and subversion reached hysterical proportions in the Post–World War II Era, making all sorts of excessive responses to the communist threat not only possible but likely. Loyalty oaths were instituted by private companies, state governments, and even the federal government, based on the apparent belief that communist spies are capable of espionage but not of lying under oath. Blacklists banned suspected subversives from work in many industries, destroying the lives of many innocent people. Alger Hiss was accused of passing government secrets to the Soviet Union. He professed his innocence to his dying day, although Soviet files released in the Post-Soviet Era suggest his guilt. The Hiss case was front-page news. Richard Nixon played a prominent role in Hiss’s prosecution, thereby earning Nixon the national spotlight for the first time.

option_explanations.A: The civil rights movement fought racial segregation and inequality (Montgomery, Selma). Loyalty oaths and blacklists belong to anti-communism, not civil rights.
option_explanations.B: The New Deal was the 1930s Depression-era reform program — a different era from the postwar anti-communist panic.
option_explanations.C: Loyalty oaths, industry blacklists, and the Alger Hiss espionage case are all hallmarks of the Second Red Scare (late 1940s-1950s), when fear of communist infiltration reached hysterical proportions.
option_explanations.D: The Great Society was Lyndon Johnson's 1960s domestic-reform program — a different era from the postwar Red Scare.

items.stem: John Foster Dulles, secretary of state under Eisenhower, intensified Cold War rhetoric with Washington’s New Look defense program that emphasized
options: threatening Moscow with “massive retaliation”
expanding conventional forces in Europe
pursuing summit diplomacy with the Soviets
conducting shuttle diplomacy in the Middle East
items.explanation: The key to this question is the phrase “intensified Cold War rhetoric.” Words like “massive retaliation” didn’t exactly improve relations with the Soviet Union. While (B), containment, was the guiding principle of U.S. foreign policy throughout the Cold War, this question is asking something more specific. And although Dulles did forge many alliances with smaller nations (collective security), (A) is a better answer. Choice (C), summit diplomacy, was practiced by Reagan and Gorbachev, while the term “shuttle diplomacy,” (D), was applied to Henry Kissinger under Nixon.

option_explanations.A: Dulles's New Look cut costly conventional forces and relied instead on nuclear deterrence — the threat that any Soviet aggression would meet 'massive retaliation.' The rhetoric sharpened the Cold War standoff.
option_explanations.B: Expanding conventional forces was the opposite of the New Look, which deliberately shrank conventional spending in favor of cheaper nuclear deterrence.
option_explanations.C: Summit diplomacy belongs to later leaders (notably Reagan and Gorbachev in the 1980s). Dulles intensified confrontation, not summitry.
option_explanations.D: Shuttle diplomacy was Henry Kissinger's Middle East diplomacy under Nixon, two decades later — not Dulles's program.

items.stem: The Cold War policy of containment and concern with national defense played a background role in the development of all of the following programs or projects EXCEPT
options: the Interstate Highway Act
the Peace Corps
the Berlin Wall
the Central Intelligence Agency
items.explanation: The influence of the policy of containment could be seen across many U.S. policies and programs, though in some not-so-obvious ways. For example, the Interstate Highway Act was intended to build a national highway system both for civilian use and to facilitate national defense, if needed: eliminate (A). The Peace Corps was created to send exemplary young Americans around the world to not only persuade young people in other countries that war wasn’t necessary—but also that the American system of capitalism created happier, healthier, more helpful citizens than communism did. This was a “soft” form of containment; eliminate (B). Likewise, while the government had established other intelligence organizations previously, the Central Intelligence Agency was founded in 1947 to not only centralize all intelligence but also to aim more specifically at gathering information about the Soviet Union. Eliminate (D). The Berlin Wall was certainly a literal type of containment, but it was built by the Soviet Union across the city of Berlin, Germany, and its construction was unrelated to the U.S. government. Choice (C) is correct.

option_explanations.A: The Interstate Highway Act (1956) was sold partly as national defense — highways for troop movement and evacuation — so containment thinking shaped it. Not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The Peace Corps (1961) was Cold War soft power: sending young Americans abroad to demonstrate capitalism's appeal against communism. Not the exception.
option_explanations.C: The Berlin Wall (1961) was built by East Germany and the Soviets to stop their own citizens from fleeing west. It was not an American containment program — this is the exception.
option_explanations.D: The CIA (1947) was created to gather Cold War intelligence against the Soviet bloc — a direct product of containment thinking. Not the exception.

items.stem: Which of the following is true regarding leftist political groups in the 1960s?
options: Their leadership tended to be female dominated in keeping with feminist ideals.
They were sharply divided in terms of those who supported the Vietnam War and those who opposed it.
They were fiercely opposed to the Warren Court on ideological grounds.
They caused a conservative backlash in the 1970s.
items.explanation: The radical leftist politics of the 1960s caused a conservative reaction in the 1970s, with the formation of many groups that advocated for a return to traditional American values on issues such as abortion, affirmative action, sexual morality, etc. However, leftist political groups in the 1960s were unified in their opposition to the Vietnam War and were ideologically aligned with the highly liberal Supreme Court under Earl Warren (although some believed the Court did not push the liberal agenda hard enough). While some groups took a strong feminist stance, most remained male-dominated, with women serving in supporting roles.

option_explanations.A: Despite feminist rhetoric, most 1960s leftist groups remained male-dominated in their leadership.
option_explanations.B: The 1960s left was unified in opposing the Vietnam War, not split between supporters and opponents of it.
option_explanations.C: The left was ideologically aligned with Earl Warren's liberal Supreme Court, not opposed to it — though some felt the Court did not go far enough.
option_explanations.D: The radicalism of the 1960s provoked a conservative backlash in the 1970s, with new organizations pushing a return to traditional values on abortion, affirmative action, and sexual morality.

options: ended with the surrender of communist forces to the Americans in 1953
resulted in substantial territorial gains for South Korea with respect to its prewar northern boundary
demonstrated that the United States was reluctant to engage China in full-blown military conflict
exemplified the willingness of the executive branch to defer to the military judgment of generals during wartime
items.explanation: President Truman, understanding the magnitude and potential consequences of going to war with communist China, refused to allow General Douglas MacArthur to launch a full-blown attack on Chinese forces when China entered the war in support of North Korea. When MacArthur publicly criticized the president for this decision, Truman fired MacArthur for insubordination—so (D) is incorrect. American troops did not advance, the parties signed an armistice in 1953, and the North–South Korean border remained at approximately the 38th parallel (the prewar boundary).

option_explanations.A: The war did not end with a communist surrender. It ended with a 1953 armistice — a ceasefire, not a surrender.
option_explanations.B: There were no substantial territorial gains. The armistice line sat near the 38th parallel, essentially the prewar boundary.
option_explanations.C: When China entered the war, Truman refused to let MacArthur launch a full-scale attack on Chinese forces, fearing a wider war — demonstrating American reluctance to engage China in all-out conflict.
option_explanations.D: Truman did not defer to his general's judgment. When MacArthur publicly criticized the president's limited-war policy, Truman fired him for insubordination.

items.stem: Which of the following does NOT accurately describe the presidential election of 1968?
options: The Democratic Party was fractured because of dissent over the Vietnam War.
A frontrunner for one of the major parties was assassinated during the primary season.
Both major-party candidates campaigned as Washington outsiders.
A third-party candidacy split the traditionally Democratic southern vote.
items.explanation: The Republican candidate, Richard Nixon, was a former vice president. The Democratic candidate, Hubert Humphrey, was the current vice president and, before that, a longtime senator. Neither could have campaigned as a Washington outsider, and neither did. The Democrats were fractured over the war; the party was home to both aggressive cold warriors and the antiwar movement. Robert Kennedy was assassinated in June; many believe he would have won the nomination had he not been killed. George Wallace formed a third party and campaigned on states’ rights and segregation, siphoning off key votes in the South, where the Democrats had traditionally done well. Nixon’s only opposition in the Republican primaries came from Nelson D. Rockefeller, who campaigned halfheartedly, and Ronald Reagan, who, at the time, was seen as too extreme to ever win the presidency. Reagan never changed, but the country did.

option_explanations.A: The Democrats were genuinely fractured over Vietnam — the 1968 Chicago convention dissolved into chaos between cold warriors and the antiwar movement. This accurately describes the election, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Robert Kennedy was genuinely assassinated in June 1968 during the primaries, when many believed he would win the nomination. This accurately describes the election, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Neither major-party candidate could plausibly run as a Washington outsider: Nixon was a former vice president and Humphrey was the sitting vice president and a longtime senator. This does not accurately describe the election — it is the exception.
option_explanations.D: George Wallace genuinely ran a third-party campaign on states' rights and segregation that split the traditionally Democratic southern vote. This accurately describes the election, so it is not the exception.

items.stem: Inflation throughout the 1970s was driven in large part by
options: the cost of funding the Vietnam War
rapidly increasing gasoline and oil prices
government investment in the space program
a dramatic reduction of income tax rates
items.explanation: Gasoline and oil prices shot through the roof in the 1970s, affecting a wide range of industries that relied on the fuels to run. The result was widespread inflation throughout the decade.

option_explanations.A: Vietnam War spending fed inflation in the late 1960s, but the 1970s inflation was driven by something else: the decade's defining shocks were energy shocks, not war spending.
option_explanations.B: The OPEC oil embargo (1973) and the 1979 energy crisis sent gasoline and oil prices soaring. Since fuel costs run through nearly every industry, the result was the decade's grinding stagflation.
option_explanations.C: Space-program spending peaked with Apollo in the 1960s. It was not the driver of 1970s inflation.
option_explanations.D: There was no dramatic income-tax cut in the 1970s — the big rate cuts came under Reagan in 1981. Tax policy did not drive the decade's inflation.

items.stem: The incident that began a chain of events that became one of the most infamous presidential scandals in American history and eventually led to the resignation of Richard Nixon was the
options: burglary of Daniel Ellsberg’s psychiatrist’s office
political sabotage of Nixon’s opponent, George McGovern
illegal use of the CIA to hush up the FBI’s investigation of the events surrounding the publication of the Pentagon Papers
break-in and attempted bugging of the Democratic Party’s national headquarters
items.explanation: This is the event that started it all—the break-in to the Watergate complex in Washington, D.C., where the Democratic Party had its national headquarters. All of the other choices became part of the cover-up and are known collectively as “Watergate,” which ultimately forced the resignation of Richard Nixon, the only president to resign in American history. Nixon resigned before he was impeached and was subsequently pardoned by Gerald Ford.

option_explanations.A: The burglary of Daniel Ellsberg's psychiatrist's office was part of the later cover-up machinery (the 'plumbers'), not the incident that started the chain.
option_explanations.B: Sabotage against McGovern was part of the campaign's covert operations against its opponents, not the incident that started the chain.
option_explanations.C: Using the CIA to block the FBI's investigation was part of the cover-up after the break-in, not the event that began the scandal.
option_explanations.D: The June 1972 break-in and attempted bugging of the Democratic National Committee's headquarters in the Watergate complex began the chain of events — investigation, cover-up, and resignation — that became the Watergate scandal.

items.stem: What was the final result of the Vietnam War?
options: The United States won a victory in the armed conflict and secured a democratic ally in the region.
The United States withdrew and the nation became a single nation united under communist rule.
The Vietnam War ended in a stalemate resulting in geographic division of the nation of Vietnam into democratic and communist nations.
The Vietnam War has never ceased and armed conflicts between democratic and communist factions within the nation continue today.
items.explanation: Under increasing social and political pressure, the United States withdrew from Vietnam and ultimately the communist-backed forces of North Vietnam secured victory and united the nation as a communist state in 1975.

option_explanations.A: The United States did not win. South Vietnam fell; there was no American victory or surviving democratic ally.
option_explanations.B: After the U.S. withdrawal (Paris accords, 1973; final evacuation, 1975), North Vietnam conquered the South and unified the country under communist rule in 1975-76.
option_explanations.C: A stalemate with permanent geographic division describes Korea, not Vietnam. Vietnam was reunified, not divided.
option_explanations.D: The war ended in 1975. Vietnam is not in a continuing democratic-vs.-communist civil war.

items.stem: A major paradox of Richard Nixon’s administration was that
options: the globalists who voted for him were disappointed by his isolationist foreign policy
the foreign powers who wanted him to end the Vietnam War were shocked when he actually extended it
his condemnation of corruption while on the campaign trail in 1968 was contradicted by his own downfall in the Watergate scandal in 1974
Nixon, a conservative Republican, enacted progressive legislation on domestic issues including workplace safety and the environment
items.explanation: While Nixon’s foreign policy was the “best of times, worst of times”—he and Secretary of State Kissinger opened China but carpetbombed Cambodia—some of his domestic policy was surprisingly liberal. He created OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration), signed the Clean Air and Clean Water acts, and established the Environmental Protection Agency. Choice (A) is a reversal: the isolationists who voted for him were disappointed by his re-engagement with China, so eliminate (A). Nixon ended the Vietnam War, which is quite the opposite of extending it, so eliminate (B). Nixon didn’t run on the idea of condemnation of corruption in 1968, so eliminate (C).

option_explanations.A: This reverses the history. Isolationists were disappointed by Nixon's re-engagement with the world — above all the opening to China — not by isolationism.
option_explanations.B: Nixon did not extend the war indefinitely; he wound down American involvement through Vietnamization and the 1973 withdrawal. The paradox here is domestic, not about extending Vietnam.
option_explanations.C: Nixon did not campaign in 1968 as an anti-corruption crusader, so Watergate-as-hypocrisy is not the paradox this item identifies.
option_explanations.D: The paradox is real: conservative Republican Nixon built a surprisingly progressive domestic record — creating the Environmental Protection Agency and OSHA, and signing the Clean Air and Clean Water Acts.
